summary: Defines how a BGP-LS speaker advertises multiple types of supported Maximum SID Depth at node or link level. This lets controllers determine whether a given SID stack can be supported in a network.

plainLanguage.summary: Each router says how long a list of instructions it can read, so the planner does not give it one that is too long.

subtitle: Two new BGP-LS TLVs let routers tell a central controller how many SIDs they can stack onto a packet.

tldr.problem: A controller computing Segment Routing paths must not build a SID stack deeper than a node can impose, but if it has no PCEP session and does not take part in IGP routing, it cannot learn the limit.
tldr.mechanism: Two new BGP-LS Attribute TLVs, Node MSD (type 266) and Link MSD (type 267), carry pairs of an MSD-Type and an MSD-Value, so BGP-LS speakers can pass on the limits learned from OSPF and IS-IS.
tldr.outcome: Controllers learn per-node and per-link Maximum SID Depth over BGP-LS. The RFC adds no new BGP operation, and a wrong advertised value can cause path computation failures.

facts.label: MSD-Value of 0
facts.value: No ability to impose any depth

today: RFC 8814 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Problem: Knowing How Deep a SID Stack Can Go
sections.content:
When a centralized controller computes Segment Routing (SR) paths, it must know the Maximum SID Depth (MSD) that each node or link can impose. Otherwise the stack of Segment Identifiers (SIDs) it builds could be longer than the node can handle.

MSD signaling already exists for PCEP (RFC 8664), OSPF (RFC 8476) and IS-IS (RFC 8491). But if PCEP is not supported or configured on the head-end of an SR tunnel, and the controller does not take part in IGP routing, the controller has no way to learn MSD. BGP-LS (RFC 7752) already exposes topology information to controllers, so this RFC extends it to carry MSD.

The RFC expects further MSD-Types in future, for example for entropy labels, and notes that in a non-SR MPLS network, MSD defines the maximum label depth.
sections.plainLanguage: A planner writes a list of steps for a messenger. Each messenger can remember only so many steps, so the planner needs to know that number first.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
MSD is the number of SIDs supported by a node or by a link on a node. A SID is a Segment Identifier as defined in RFC 8402.

Label imposition is the act of modifying and/or adding labels to the outgoing label stack of a packet. It includes replacing the label at the top of the stack and pushing new labels. The number of labels imposed is the sum of those replaced and those pushed.
sections.plainLanguage: MSD is how many instruction cards a router can stick on a packet at once.

sections.title: Advertising MSD via BGP-LS
sections.content:
The extensions let BGP-LS speakers tell a consumer of topology data, such as a centralized controller, about the MSD capabilities of nodes and their links. The controller can use this when computing SR paths.

When a speaker originates topology learned through OSPF or IS-IS, the MSD information comes from the underlying IGP extensions in RFC 8476 and RFC 8491. The TLVs can carry any MSD-Type from the "IGP MSD-Types" registry introduced in RFC 8491, including types defined later by the IGPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers already tell each other their limits. This RFC lets them pass those limits on to the planner too.

sections.title: The Node MSD TLV
sections.content:
The Node MSD TLV is a new Node Attribute TLV with Type 266. It carries the provisioned SID depth of the router identified by the Router-ID. Node MSD is the smallest MSD supported by the node on the set of interfaces configured for use. Values may be learned through a hardware API or provisioned.

The Length field is variable, a multiple of 2, and is the total length of the value in octets. The value is one or more pairs of a 1-octet MSD-Type and a 1-octet MSD-Value.

MSD-Value is a number from 0 to 255. A value of 0 means the node cannot impose an MSD stack of any depth. Any other value MUST be the lowest value supported by any link configured for use by the advertising protocol instance.
sections.plainLanguage: The node says one number for the whole router: the smallest number any of its doors can handle.

sections.title: The Link MSD TLV
sections.content:
The Link MSD TLV is a new Link Attribute TLV with Type 267. It carries the MSD of the interface associated with the link. Its layout is the same as the Node MSD TLV: a variable Length that is a multiple of 2, followed by pairs of a 1-octet MSD-Type and a 1-octet MSD-Value.

The MSD-Value range is again 0 to 255, with 0 meaning no ability to impose an MSD stack of any depth. Any other value is the MSD of the link when used as an outgoing interface.
sections.plainLanguage: A link gets its own number too, because one door may handle fewer instructions than the router as a whole.

sections.title: IANA Code Points
sections.content: IANA assigned the two TLV code points in the registry "BGP-LS Node Descriptor, Link Descriptor, Prefix Descriptor, and Attribute TLVs". The table also records the matching IS-IS TLV or sub-TLV: Node MSD maps to 242/23, and Link MSD maps to (22,23,25,141,222,223)/15.
sections.plainLanguage: The two new labels were written into the official list, each with its own number.

sections.title: Manageability
sections.content:
The extensions only add new Attribute TLVs and do not affect BGP operation beyond what RFC 7752 already covers. The malformed-attribute checks of RFC 7752 now include these TLVs, and a syntax error in them causes the BGP-LS Attribute to be discarded. Checking the meaning of the TLVs is left to the consumer, such as a controller, and not the BGP protocol.

Encoding or decoding errors may leave a PCE without the information, or with incorrect information, so a head-end may be unable to instantiate the desired SR path. How applications handle this is implementation specific and out of scope. The RFC adds no new BGP or BGP-LS configuration or monitoring.
sections.plainLanguage: If a number gets scrambled, the planner might hand a router a list that is too long. How the planner copes is up to the planner.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An incorrect MSD value can do harm. If it is smaller than what is supported, path computation may fail to find a viable path. If it is larger, a path may be attempted that the head-end cannot support. The presence of this information may also show an attacker how to induce either condition.

The extensions do not change the BGP security model. The TLVs propagate the IGP MSD extensions, and it is assumed the IGP instances that originate them provide the required security. The RFC concludes that the new information adds no significant risk beyond the node and link attribute information already supported in RFC 7752.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone lies about the number, the planner makes bad plans. So the number needs to come from a source you trust.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the value field in octets; a multiple of 2.

fields.name: MSD-Type
fields.desc: A value from the IGP MSD-Types registry.

fields.name: MSD-Value
fields.desc: 0 to 255; 0 means no ability to impose any depth.

fields.name: More pairs
fields.desc: Further MSD-Type and MSD-Value pairs may follow.
